15	- **gap ledger**: File with one numbered row for each known gap or defect.
16	
17	## 1. The start and the exploring era (08-19 to 09-16)
18	
19	### The 2012 tree builds and runs again
20	
21	- 08-18 and 08-19: the tree built on JDK 8, and the team's tests ran: about 1.4K in `testFast`, 382 in `testSystem`.
22	- 08-19: the first toy programs ran under walk: a small demo, a Mandelbrot set ported from Swift and rewritten in plain Fortress style, and a ring of complex numbers.
23	- To 08-21: the build moved to current Java and Scala. These 21 commits change nothing a Fortress programmer sees. The suites ran in parallel, 13 minutes down to 7.5.
24	
25	**The microGPT rounds (08-23 to 08-30).** microGPT is Karpathy's small GPT in Python. Each round wrote it in Fortress and ran it under walk. A golden check compared its numbers with the Python program's.
26	
27	- Round 1 (08-23): a direct port. A training step took 10.9 s, against 22 ms in Python.
28	- 08-24 to 08-30: rewrites in plain Fortress style and in a paper's mathematical style, then a second iteration. The session began to use worker agents.
29	
30	**Other assistants (09-07 to 09-11).** Astra, an OpenAI model running in Codex, wrote its own port outside this session, with no transcript. Later Astra and Sol, a second OpenAI model, joined a discussion of notation.
31	
32	### Blinded and informed runs (09-08 to 09-15)
33	
34	- The blinded run (09-08): a fresh session that could not read the earlier ports. It worked alone for 1.5 hours and wrote 15 gap rows.
35	- Run B (09-09) could read the earlier work: 25 gap rows. Run B2, the coordinating session's own attempt: 39 rows.
36	- Runs C to C4 (09-14) used a "flat" layout, after Hsu's data design for array languages. C4 merged C2 and C3: a 71-line model passing 40 of 40 checks.
37	- The APL side quest (to 09-15): APL notation turned into Fortress code by a grammar extension, then microGPT written in it. The curator closed the quest there.
38	
39	**The ledger's first 309 rows.** Each run wrote a gap table. A merge worker re-ran every reproducer, numbered the rows and folded repeats: 83 rows on 09-08, 139 after Runs B and B2, 265 after the APL merge, rows 288 to 310 on 09-16. Row 148 is empty on purpose. `FACTS.md` (what is established) and `POSITIONS.md` (the curator's decisions) began on 09-15.
40	
41	**The territory map (09-16).** Before the revival edited the team's language, five surveys described the system: modules, what of the specification is built, tests, dormant code, and the designers' reasons. Two of its facts: the interpreter's tests and the compiler's tests share no program; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the team's Working Draft as of 2011-02-02, and `Specification/` is the text the revival revises.
42	
43	**The sealed tree.** The tag `sealed-tree` (`75cca6683`, 09-16) marks the map's last commit. After it, the revival edits the team's language, library and specification.
44	
45	Sources: `explorations/process-records/01-microgpt-port.md` to `14-apl-rung-4b.md`; `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`; `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover-history.md`; `explorations/coordinator/map/README.md`; `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 1.1; `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/fortress-changes-chronology.md` A0, A1, A10; `explorations/notation-collaboration/README.md`.
46	
47	## 2. The unsealed tree and the batches (09-17 to 10-10)
48	
49	**How a batch works.** A batch is one run of a workflow script.
50	
51	- A **rung** is one piece of work, done by a worker in its own checkout of the tree.
52	- A **skeptic** checks each rung. Up to batch 10, if it refused, a **judge** ruled, a **repair** agent fixed, and a second skeptic checked. Since batch 11 the skeptic fixes what it finds, and a judge rules only on a contested fix.
53	- The **gather** folds each rung's notes into the record. A **merged-diff review** reads the combined change.
54	- The **gate** is the full check before landing: the build, both suites, compiled `atomic` programs at four threads, the ladder (below), and the checker's error counts. To **land** is to commit to `main` and push.
55	- After each batch, one reviewer checks it against the decisions and the designers' intent.
56	
57	**The first climbs (09-17 to 09-20).** The ladder is 410 of the team's test programs pushed through the compiled path. On the sealed tree 59 passed.
58	
59	- The ladder climb (09-17): eight rungs added names to the prelude and compiled a top-level `var`. 81 passed. A review found one rung against the specification and one departing from it without a reason.
60	- The repair batch (09-18 to 09-19) fixed those two.
61	- Batches 1 and 2 (09-19, 09-20) added more prelude names: `RR64`'s functions, `Maybe`, `GCD`, shifts, integer conversions. 85 passed, and 85 still pass.
62	
63	**Batches 3 to 10 (09-22 to 10-03).** From 09-21 every batch worked to make the checker accept the one library: 16 landings in 12 days. Names such as 3.5, 6b, 7R, N or 7b are batches split from or added to a plan. Batches 8 to 10 repaired checker defects and the library's one-off slips. The decisions below say which batch built each one. Batches 11, 12 and 13 landed on 10-09, and 13b on 10-10 (part 4).
64	
65	### The main decisions, in plain words
66	
67	- **The goal** (09-16). Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification as revised. The measure is microGPT compiled and running fast. The tree was unsealed on 09-17.
68	- **Test first** (09-17). Every edit starts from a failing test that stays in the suite. Expected-failure tests in the interpreter's suite (files named `XXX…`) grew from 56 to 120.
69	- **One library** (09-21). The interpreter's library becomes the only one. The prelude gets no new declaration and goes at the switch-over. The rungs that added prelude names stopped, and the checker's errors on the one library became the measure.
70	- **The flat number tower** (09-24). The checker keeps the team's rule that no type extends two instantiations of one generic trait. The one library's nested number types broke it, so they became siblings that convert by declared coercions, as in the prelude. Walk learned coercion in batch 4; the library was flattened in batch 6. The checker's errors fell from 125 to 62.
71	- **Sizes at run time** (09-24). A size parameter (`nat`) gets the run-time descriptor a type argument has. Since batch 5, a sized program compiles and runs.
72	- **Overflow** (09-26). Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk too. Code meant to wrap uses the specification's operators ∔ ∸ ⨰. Batches 5 and 6b.
73	- **The plan** (09-26). Six phases: 1 and 2, decided work and the flattening; 3, the checker at zero errors; 4, the switch-over; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. Phase 3 has landed through batch 13b; phases 4 to 6 have not started.
74	- **Ranges over `ZZ32` only**, because a JVM array index is a 32-bit integer. Batch 7R.
75	- **The inference rule.** When a generic call mixes number types, the type parameter takes the narrowest type all arguments convert into. A parameter that nothing in a call fixes is inferred at its bound, not at the empty type `Bottom`, on both paths, with a few cases left under walk; at run time the rule is only partly built (part 6). Batches N, 8, 9 and 11.
76	- **The overloading model.** Overloads may differ in static parameters. The return-type rule is checked for every instance. Walk chooses by declared types, not by order in the file. Batch 7b.
77	- **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** Batch 7.
78	- **Arrays become unboxed `double[]`** (09-19). Decided, not built.
79	- **Each change to the specification** gets a callout at the passage and an Appendix I entry with the original text and the reason.
80	
81	**The checker's errors falling.** Two numbers measure the way to the switch-over.
82	
83	- **The checker count**: the errors the checker reports on the one library. The checker stops at the first error of some checks, so the count misses errors behind the stop. A gate stage from batch 3.
84	- **The distance to the switch-over**: every error over all the library's files, with no early stop. First measured before batch 7.
85	- Neither makes the gate red. A fix can raise both, when it lets the checker reach code it could not reach before.
86	
87	**The checker count, where it moved**
88	
89	- before batch 3: 93
90	- after 3: 103
91	- after 4: 125 (a fixed crash showed 22 hidden errors)
92	- after 6: 62 (the flat number tower)
93	- after 7: 22
94	- after 7R: 10
95	- after 7C: 75 (the checker now reads a clause it used to stop at)
96	- after 7b: 59
97	- after 8: 56
98	- after 9 to 12: 1 (a pair in `LexicographicReduction` (row 582), left for the curator's choice)
99	- after 13, 13b: 1 (the pair fixed; now an untyped parameter)
100	
101	**The distance to the switch-over, where it moved**
102	
103	- before batch 7: 1.7K (first measured)
104	- after 7: 940
105	- after 7R: 627
106	- after 7b: 598
107	- after 8: 565
108	- after 9: 340
109	- after 10: 253
110	- after 11: 207
111	- after 12: 153
112	- after 13: 105
113	- after 13b: 85
114	
115	Of the 85: 29 are bodies over the self-typed `Integral` trait, which wait for a judgement on how to type them; 19 are in the array family; 16 are one-off slips and limits of the checker.
116	
117	**Where the tokens went.** "Written" means tokens processed fresh: cache writes and new input, the measure the curator uses.
118	
119	- The 15 batches from the repair batch to 6.5b used 269 agents and wrote 146M tokens.
120	- Rung workers took about half; skeptics, judges, repairs and reviews about two-fifths.
121	- 45% of all writes came after an agent waited five minutes or more. The prompt cache lives five minutes, so the agent wrote its whole context again.
122	- The largest batches: 7 (22M), N (18M), 6.5b (17M). After the post-mortem: 7b 7.3M, 8 and 9 14.6M together, 10 6.3M.
123	
124	### Where the records went: the post-mortem of 09-29
125	
126	- Batch 6.5b changed about 280 lines of Fortress code, 90 of specification and 710 of tests. Beside them it committed 866 record files, 46K lines, most of them scratch.
127	- Nobody had asked the curator whether scratch goes to `main`. It came from six small steps. On 09-19 he asked whether logs were needed. Gate logs stayed out, but rung outputs were then named `.txt`, so `.gitignore` missed them, and he was not told.
128	- Two cleanings removed 4.4K files (11.7 MB) on 09-29 and 9.9K files (173 MB) on 09-30.
129	- The new practice: commit only what `main` is to hold; write the test and see it fail first; build or run nothing twice. Batch 7b committed 20 record files.
130	
131	Sources: `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md` and `-history.md`; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md` ("Where we stand", "The phases"), `POSITIONS.md`, `FACTS.md` (the distance by root cause); `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-29/README.md` and `characterization.md`; `explorations/reviews/batch-6.5-review.md` to `batch-13-review.md`; `explorations/compile-ladder/CLIMB.md` and `climb-batch-13b/RECORD.md`; `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/README.md`; `git ls-tree` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`.
132	
133	## 3. How the record grew
134	
135	![The gap ledger's characters and rows, and FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX, commit by commit from 09-08 to 10-09, with each batch's landing marked](record-growth/record-growth.png)
136	
137	The chart has three panels on one time axis. A vertical line marks each batch's landing. Top: the ledger's characters. Middle: its rows. Bottom: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (INDEX has one line for each note under `explorations/`).
138	
139	- The ledger reached `main` on 09-09 with 83 rows. It reached 638 rows and 1.25M characters at batch 10 (10-03). At batch 13 it had 694 rows and 581K characters.
140	- The exploring era wrote 309 rows, 0.8K characters each on average. At batch 13 they held 247K characters.
141	- The batches wrote 329 rows to batch 10. At entry they were two to three times as long: 2.6K on average in the first batches, 1.4K in batches 8 to 10. Later edits made them 40% to 55% longer, to 0.88M characters on 10-03. At batch 13 they held 275K. The 56 rows added since batch 10 hold 49K, 0.9K each on average.
142	- So most of the ledger's text still comes from the batches' rows, not from the exploring era's: 275K against 247K.
143	- Rows almost never shrank until 10-08: after entry they gained 308K characters and lost 0.8K. Then the ledger was rewritten. Each row was cut to 1,200 characters at most, and the ledger fell from 1.25M to 541K characters in one commit. The mean row went from 1.9K to 0.8K. The earlier text is in a history file, 1.33M characters. Closing a row cuts it too.
144	- From 09-17 to batch 13, batch runs took 28% of the clock (35% to batch 10; no batch ran from 10-03 to 10-08). They brought 89% of the ledger's new characters and 93% of its new rows (88% and 92% to batch 10).
145	- FACTS peaked at 352K at batch 7b (09-30). On 10-02 it lost 92K in one commit, when the rung entries were cut to the fact. It was 294K at batch 13.
146	- POSITIONS peaked at 105K (09-29) and was 94K at batch 13. INDEX never lost more than 324 characters in a commit, and stands at 175K.
147	
148	Sources: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-growth/README.md`, `per-batch.csv`, `series.csv`, `landings.csv`; `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` sections 1.1 and 2.4; `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
149	
150	## 4. Since 10-04: the skills and the process
151	
152	**The process-engineering study** (opened 10-03) asks whether the weekly token pool is spent well.
153	
154	- Sharing one build between checkouts had been called impossible for two weeks. Given the goal, fresh agents found the way in about 15 minutes. The waste was 245 of 425 builds, about 7.3 agent-hours.
155	- One probe wrote 7.0M tokens against an estimate of 0.5M. Now the coordinator watches a long run against its estimate.
156	- Six designs for running batch 10 were priced: four at 4.5M to 7.5M, two with no cost limit at about 31M and 37M. Whether to design a workflow for each batch waits on the curator.
157	- 10-08: the round after a skeptic refuses was redesigned (part 2).
158	
159	**The `fortress-repo` skill**: the instructions every agent loads to work here.
160	
161	- 10-04: three project skills written from the record and reviewed.
162	- 10-05: a reader given only the skill found about 30 passages a new reader could not act on.
163	- 10-05 and 10-06: the curator reviewed it, about 35 comments, grouped as eight lenses. A writer applied them, and every file got shorter.
164	- 10-07: the skill gained two modes of work, building and exploring.
165	- 10-08: a fresh session answered a quiz on Fortress from pre-training alone; an audit graded 56 claims correct, 7 wrong, 3 outdated. The section "Fortress as a language" came from it.
166	
167	**The context study** (10-08): what batch 10's four rung workers read before their first fix.
168	
169	- Of what they read: the briefing 25%; code, library, specification and tests 48%; their own searches of the record 4%.
170	- Relearning what the record held was common but small: about 1% of what they read.
171	- A "librarian" pass after each batch would cost 0.7M to 0.9M tokens. It pays if it turns the causes of refusals into skill rules.
172	
173	### The ledger
174	
175	- An archaeology (10-08) proposed a form. The curator decided: one status word of seven, a class with its area, at most 1.2K characters a row, topic sections with every number kept, the old text in a history file, one tool, `ledger.py`, to write it.
176	- The ledger check (10-08) compared about 490 rows with the batch records and found three mismatches.
177	- The rewrite landed on 10-08 at 14:06. The 638 rows kept their numbers and stand in fifteen topic sections (part 3).
178	
179	**The climb** paused from 10-03 to 10-08 while this work ran. Batch 11 began at 23:42 on 10-08.
180	
181	Sources: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/README.md`, `batch-redesign.md`, `context-study.md`, `ledger-check.md`, `gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, `skill-effect.md` section 1; `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`; `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md` (the ledger's form, the skills); `git show -s ae4f8e38a`.
182	
183	## 5. What the revival changed in Fortress itself
184	
185	Changes a programmer writing Fortress would notice, by area.
186	
187	### Numbers
188	
189	- The number types are siblings under `Number`, not a tower, as the team's compiler library already had them. A wider type converts from a narrower one by a declared `coerce`.
190	- Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk, as on the compiled path. To wrap on purpose, write ∔, ∸ or ⨰.
191	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic. Under walk, a reduction whose element type nothing fixes runs. The checker still needs it written: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] f(j)`.
192	- `QQ` is exact. A negative shift count shifts the other way. `GCD` and `LCM` are never negative. `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits. `round` sends an exact half to the even integer.
193	- The library's numeral type is `IntLiteral`, a sibling that the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` convert from. Walk's numerals are unchanged for now.
194	
195	**Ranges.** Ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` or `ZZ` stops when built. A subscript of rank 2 or 3 is checked corner by corner, so a corner outside the bounds raises `IndexOutOfBounds`.
196	
197	### Arrays and the rest of the library
198	
199	- `fill` takes a value; `tabulate` takes a function.
200	- The array types bound their elements: `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.
201	- `String`'s juxtaposition is three top-level operators.
202	- Array storage is still boxed.
203	
204	### Walk
205	
206	- Walk converts by coercion at calls, bindings and assignments, picking the coercion from the run-time value.
207	- Walk infers type arguments through coercions. A type parameter nothing fixes takes its bound, and one whose bound names itself stays open.
208	- Walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration by declared types, not by order in the file.
209	- At load, walk refuses some programs it used to run: an object extending two closed traits without being listed; two functional methods with no declaration on their meet; an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, as five of the team's demos do; an `override` that overrides nothing.
210	
211	### The checker
212	
213	- It checks `nat` and `int` size parameters, arithmetic in a size and a size known only at run time, and infers static arguments through coercions.
214	- Overloads may differ in static parameters. The return-type rule is checked for every instance.
215	- It judges two functional methods for each type that provides both.
216	
217	### The code generator and the run time
218	
219	- A top-level `var` compiles, and `atomic` covers it.
220	- A numeral of exactly 32 or 64 bits keeps its value.
221	- A sized program compiles, loads and runs. Generic code dispatches correctly on four threads.
222	- An object with no `asString` prints its type name.
223	
224	**The specification.** Appendix I has 39 entries, each with the original text and the reason.
225	
226	### Size of the internal changes
227	
228	- 143 commits touched the code, library or specification: 28 before the tag, 21 of them toolchain; 115 after it.
229	- Lines added after the tag: walk 3.3K, checker 1.8K, code generator and run time 1.0K, specification 5.3K, tests 14.5K. The library gained 3.6K lines and lost 2.3K.
230	- The grammar is unchanged. The suites grew from about 1.4K and 382 tests to 1.9K and 580.
231	
232	Sources: `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/fortress-changes-chronology.md` part A (to batch 10); `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`; `climb-batch-13b/gate/summary.txt`; `git diff --numstat 75cca6683 main`.
233	
234	## 6. The original Fortress and the revival's resolutions
235	
236	### Custodians, not authors
237	
238	The first principle of the protocol the work follows reads: "We are custodians of their language, not its authors." It asks the revival to finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification and by the library's own practice. Every agent is bound by the same rules through the skill it loads.
239	
240	- No committed file claims credit for the revival.
241	- Where git doesn't record who wrote something, the authorship is rebuilt from the history. It's never guessed.
242	- Reasons go into commit messages and reports, not into the team's source comments.
243	- Every claim is checked against a primary source: the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output.
244	
245	None of the team's tests or demos was deleted, and 43 were edited, each for a reason on record.
246	
247	### The team left three sources that disagree
248	
249	The team left Fortress in three forms, with the type papers beside them:
250	
251	- the specification, the text that says what Fortress is;
252	- the interpreter (walk) and its library;
253	- the compiler and its own, smaller library.
254	
255	These disagree in places. The revival changes the team's Fortress for one of two reasons only: two of these sources contradict each other, or a program fails. It reconciles them. Where the team's later work, in the compiler's library or the type papers, departs from the original specification, the revival follows the later work. It then updates the specification to match what it implements. A callout marks the passage, and Appendix I keeps the original text with the reason.
256	
257	### Example: the number types
258	
259	- The team's interpreter library put the number types in a tower. A narrower type was a kind of the wider type: `ZZ32` was a kind of `ZZ64`, and `ZZ64` a kind of `ZZ`.
260	- The prelude went from siblings to a tower and back in 2009. Christine Flood declared its widths as sibling objects in March. Jan-Willem Maessen made them a tower later that month. David Chase cut the subtyping between the widths in August. Sukyoung Ryu added the first exclusion, `ZZ32 excludes ZZ64`, in October. Maessen and Eric Allen widened the exclusions and added the first coercions, from November 2009 to January 2010. Guy Steele built the comparisons and the integer operators on the flat prelude in 2011.
261	- In 2010 Justin Hilburn built the exclusion rule into the checker: no type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. In the tower, `ZZ32` is both an `Integral` of `ZZ32` and, through `ZZ64`, an `Integral` of `ZZ64`, which the rule refuses. The siblings obey it.
262	- On 09-24 the curator chose to keep the rule. Batch 6 made the interpreter's library siblings too, on 09-27, so that the checker accepts it.
263	
264	So a model that remembers the tower remembers the team's interpreter library correctly. What it doesn't know is that the team's compiler had left the tower in 2009.
265	
266	### Left as the team had it
267	
268	- Functional methods: a method with `self` among its parameters is called as `f(x)`.
269	- Juxtaposition as an operator, and the whitespace rules. The grammar is unchanged.
270	- Declarations: `x = e`, `var x: T = e`, `x := e`.
271	- Loops and reductions are library code. A `for` loop, a comprehension and `SUM` turn into calls to library objects: a generator, which produces the values, and a reduction, which combines them.
272	- Evaluation is parallel by default. The revival pins the suites to four threads in the build file.
273	- Only the compiled path checks static types. Walk checks more when it loads a program, but these aren't static types.
274	- What the specification describes and the team never built is still unbuilt: dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions, reduction variables, complex numbers.
275	
276	### Where the revival resolved a contradiction
277	
278	#### Dispatch on every argument
279	
280	- **Overloads that differ in static parameters.**
281	  - Original: one sentence of the Working Draft forbids this. The 1.0 release of March 2008 doesn't have it. In git, the sentence first appears in the specification's sources as Sukyoung Ryu re-imported them in November 2009. Neither implementation enforced it. The checker implements the type group's model of 2011, from their OOPSLA paper, which allows such overloads.
282	  - Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the 2011 model. The implementations and the library already overload across static parameters, and enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
283	- **The return-type rule.**
284	  - Original: the 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one. A pair that broke the rule then passed the checker and failed the JVM's check of the bytecode.
285	  - Resolution: the checker tests every instance, as the paper asks. Such a program now fails when it's compiled, not when it runs.
286	- **How walk chooses between a generic and a plain declaration.**
287	  - Original: the specification chooses by the declarations' types. Walk chose by their order in the file.
288	  - Resolution: walk now chooses by the declared types, as the specification says. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
289	
290	#### Traits and objects
291	
292	- **The exclusion rule.**
293	  - Original: the checker has enforced the rule since 2010, and the 2011 paper states it. The Working Draft doesn't, and some of its examples break it.
294	  - Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed". Without the rule, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`.
295	- **What a `comprises` clause says.**
296	  - Original: four passages of the Working Draft read it as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs it allows. The Types chapter of the 2012 restart reads it as a statement about values.
297	  - Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. Read by values, the passages hold.
298	
299	#### Static parameters
300	
301	- **The bound of a type parameter with no written bound.**
302	  - Original: the Working Draft says `Object`. The library uses its generic containers with tuples, which `Object` doesn't hold, and writes `Any` where it states a bound.
303	  - Resolution: the bound is `Any`, because the library works only with `Any`.
304	- **A type parameter that nothing in a call fixes.**
305	  - Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's check of the bytecode. The POPL 2019 paper of Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu gives such a parameter its bound, never `Bottom`.
306	  - Built: the specification states the paper's rule. The checker infers such a parameter at its bounds, never at `Bottom`. Walk gives it its declared bound, and leaves open one whose bound names itself, such as `SUM`'s. Walk still gives `Bottom` in four narrow cases.
307	  - Not built yet: at run time both implementations still run a dispatched generic declaration at the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter. The compiled path waits for phase 5, when its dispatcher will carry the call's static return type.
308	- **Sizes on the compiled path.** The specification has size parameters. The compiled path couldn't carry them, but its code generator had a slot reserved for them. The revival fills the reserved slot, in the team's pattern for type arguments, and a program with sizes now compiles and runs.
309	
310	#### Numbers
311	
312	- **Conversion in walk.** The specification says that a call converts its arguments when that makes it apply. Walk had a note "TODO add checks for COERCE" at that place. Walk now converts the arguments, doing the work the team's note left to do.
313	- **Overflow.** The specification and the compiled path raise `IntegerOverflow` when a fixed-width result doesn't fit; walk wrapped the result. Walk now raises it too. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's own wrapping operators.
314	- **Ranges.** The interpreter's ranges took any integer type, the prelude's only `ZZ32`. Ranges are now over `ZZ32` only, as in the prelude, since a JVM array index is a 32-bit integer.
315	- **`SUM` and `PROD`.** `SUM` used catch-all operators on `Number`, which went with the tower. `SUM` and `PROD` are now one generic declaration each, over the element type's own algebra.
316	
317	### Where the quiz was right about the original
318	
319	A fresh model answered a quiz on Fortress from its training alone (part 4). The audit graded each answer against today's tree, so an answer can be right about the team's Fortress and still be graded down:
320	
321	- The quiz didn't say how the number types relate. A reader who assumes a tower, narrower below wider, describes the team's interpreter library exactly.
322	- Its answer that overflow raises an error, graded correct, holds for the team's specification and compiler. The team's walk wrapped.
323	
324	Some answers marked wrong come from the team's own specification, which describes more than the team built:
325	
326	- `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]` with laws: a chapter of the specification. The library has it only in a comment and in its incomplete folder.
327	- `fortress run Foo.fss`: the specification's overview says this. The team's tool runs a program under walk with `fortress Foo.fss`.
328	- Complex numbers: named in the specification, in no library.
329	- Tests that state their expected output: the team's compiler tests do this. Its interpreter tests don't.
330	
331	Two answers are wrong for both the team and the revival: integer types that wrap by themselves (the specification wraps only with its own operators), and an `Any` type that doesn't hold tuples. One more is wrong for the team: the guess that walk built part of the coercion rules. The team's walk had none.
332	
333	Sources: `explorations/protocol.md` (principle 1); `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`; `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md` (the flattening, the exclusion rule, the static-parameter sentence, the instance rule); `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex` lines 100 to 108; `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/spec-sentences-dated.md`; `git diff --diff-filter=M` and `=D a874948ac main` over the team's test and demo folders; `explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`; `skills-distillation-audit.md` section B; the team's commits, read with `git show -s`: b2880c05c, 76c267f98, 6896886fb, 3e0306166, 128f313b5, 2ef730c88, d0cde7d17, b3c2e1342, da5291587, d535963cb (the prelude's numbers); 5a6b7913b, e828b44b1 (the exclusion rule in the checker); cec470a34, 0f49d8698 (the static-parameter sentence); 166841592, 275b90773 (the 2012 restart).

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
